title: A Daughter Who Wants to Remove the Veil
scenario: Yasmin Khalil, 19, a first-year student in Cairo, tells her older cousin Dalal that she wishes to stop wearing the hijab. Her father, a respected shopkeeper, would be shamed in his community and may restrict her studies. Dalal, 31, is the only person Yasmin has confided in and is asked by Yasmin to speak to the father on her behalf. Dalal fears that stepping in could backfire. She must decide how to respond this week.
options: Speak to the father and advocate for Yasmin's right to choose, accepting the risk of family conflict and consequences for Dalal herself.
Advise Yasmin to wait until she is financially independent before acting, prioritising her safety and education over immediate authenticity.
Decline to get involved and encourage Yasmin to speak for herself, respecting boundaries but leaving her alone with the risk.

title: The Naming Ceremony Dispute
scenario: Kwabena and Esi Boateng's newborn son is due to have an outdoor Akan naming ceremony on the eighth day. Esi, a recent convert to a Pentecostal church, objects to the libation, which her pastor calls idol worship. Kwabena's elderly father, the family head, insists that the ritual is essential and not a religious act but an introduction to the ancestors. Kwabena, 33, must tell his father tonight whether the libation will happen.
options: Insist on the traditional libation, honouring his father and the lineage and treating Esi's objection as secondary to the child's belonging.
Skip the libation to respect Esi's conscience, accepting his father's displeasure and the possible rift in the family.
Hold the ceremony with the libation performed by his father outside Esi's presence, trying to honour both but risking a sense of evasion.

title: Fasting Through Chemotherapy
scenario: Mustafa Demir, a 52-year-old Turkish baker in Berlin, is receiving chemotherapy for lymphoma. Ramadan begins next week and he intends to fast fully. His oncologist, Dr. Weiss, warns that fasting could cause dangerous dehydration and interfere with treatment timing. The imam at his mosque says illness exempts him but Mustafa feels shame at not fasting. His wife, Gul, begs him to follow medical advice. Mustafa must decide how to plan the month.
options: Fast despite the risk, treating this as his own conscientious religious choice and accepting the health consequences.
Follow the exemption and skip fasting, accepting the guidance of the doctor and imam and living with his feelings of shame.
Fast partially on days without treatment under medical monitoring, trying to honour both concerns at some added risk.

title: Cut or Uncut
scenario: In a village in the Gambia, Fatou Jallow is told by her mother-in-law that the girls in the family undergo traditional cutting at age ten, as a mark of belonging and marriageability. Fatou, a midwife who has seen the complications, wishes to spare her daughter. If she refuses, her daughter may face stigma and Fatou may be ostracised. A health NGO worker offers a symbolic ritual without cutting. Fatou must tell her mother-in-law her decision before the coming ceremony.
options: Refuse outright, protecting her daughter from bodily harm despite the social consequences for them both.
Propose the alternative symbolic ritual to her mother-in-law, hoping to preserve belonging without the harm, though it may be rejected.
Seek the guidance of a respected elder who is sympathetic to change, delaying the conflict but risking the ceremony date passing.

title: The Arranged Introductions
scenario: Meera Joshi, 27, a software tester in Pune, has been quietly dating a classmate from a different caste. Her parents have begun arranged introductions with families of their own community and her father's health is poor. Meera's brother Anand, 30, knows about the relationship and is asked by his mother whether Meera is seeing anyone. Anand must answer his mother at dinner tonight, and he knows his answer may shape how the family handles Meera's life.
options: Tell his mother the truth, believing deception within the family damages trust and that Meera should be supported openly.
Say he knows nothing, protecting Meera's privacy and giving her time to speak for herself.
Tell his mother that Meera should be the one to answer, without confirming or denying, avoiding a direct lie but possibly signalling the truth.

title: Sabbath and the Exam Timetable
scenario: Principal Rebecca Katz of a Jewish day school in Melbourne finds that a state exam for her senior students falls on Saturday. Most families will keep Shabbat, but a few students and parents want to take the test, saying their futures cannot wait. Some rabbis permit it in limited circumstances; others do not. A student, Noam, 17, asks her to support his choice to sit the exam. She must decide what the school will announce.
options: Support the exam sitting for those who choose to take it, respecting individual conscience and rabbinic diversity.
Tell all students to observe Shabbat and seek a rescheduled sitting, upholding the school's religious identity.
Leave the decision to families and offer no official position, staying neutral but risking social pressure on individual students.
tension: communal religious identity vs. individual conscience

title: Blood and the Surgeon's Dilemma
scenario: Dr. Pavel Horvat, a surgeon in Zagreb, must operate on a 34-year-old woman, Mirela, a Jehovah's Witness, for a ruptured ectopic pregnancy complication. She is conscious and refuses blood products on religious grounds. Her husband, also a Witness, supports her. Her mother, who is not a Witness, pleads with Dr. Horvat to ignore the refusal. Surgery without transfusion carries a greater risk of death. Dr. Horvat must decide how to proceed in the next ten minutes.
options: Honour Mirela's refusal and operate using blood-sparing techniques only, accepting a higher risk of death.
Prepare for transfusion if she loses consciousness, concluding that saving her life should override a refusal she may reconsider.
Spend a few more minutes confirming her wishes in private, apart from family, before deciding, risking a delay in treatment.

title: Shaving the Child's Head
scenario: Akira Tanabe and Daniela Moretti, a Japanese-Italian couple in Turin, are expecting a baby. Akira's mother wants the baby to wear a traditional Shinto amulet from a shrine and to be presented there at one month. Daniela, raised Catholic and now a committed atheist, finds the ritual hypocritical but also sees it as meaningful to Akira's mother. Akira, an engineer, is caught between them and must tell his mother by next week.
options: Agree to the shrine visit as a cultural rather than religious act, valuing his mother's feelings and the child's heritage.
Decline the visit, standing with Daniela's convictions and deferring any religious exposure until the child can choose.
Offer a family blessing at home with no religious element, trying to honour his mother's love without the ritual.

title: Hair, Honour and the Military
scenario: Sergeant Harpreet Singh Gill, 29, serves in the Canadian Armed Forces and has kept his hair uncut as a Sikh. His unit is training for deployment to a chemical-hazard zone where a gas-mask seal requires a clean-shaven face. His commanding officer, Major Tremblay, offers a non-deploying role. Harpreet's grandfather says that to give up the kesh would be a betrayal. Harpreet must give the Major his answer by Friday.
options: Decline deployment and take the non-deploying role, keeping his faith practice intact at the cost of career and comradeship.
Shave for the deployment after consulting a Sikh scholar about exceptions, accepting his grandfather's disapproval for what he sees as necessary duty.
Ask for an alternative protective equipment fit, risking delay and rejection, but seeking to fulfil both commitments.

title: Sky Burial at the Border
scenario: Tenzin Dolma, a 40-year-old nurse in Lhasa, learns that her father has died and the family plans a traditional sky burial. New local regulations limit the practice, and a neighbour suggests the authorities might punish those involved. Her brother, a monk, insists the ritual is essential for his father's rebirth. Her young husband fears for his job in the government office. Tenzin must say whether she will take part in the preparations.
options: Take part and arrange the sky burial discreetly, prioritising the father's spiritual needs and the family's faith.
Choose cremation in a licensed facility with prayers by the monks, avoiding legal risk while still offering rites.
Refuse any plan that risks the family, leaving it to her brother and standing aside from the decision.

title: Cousin Marriage and the Genetic Counsellor
scenario: Counsellor Shirin Taheri in Tehran meets two cousins, Reza and Maryam, planning marriage as their families wish. Their family has a history of thalassemia, and testing shows both are carriers. Their grandmothers insist cousin marriage is a blessed tradition. Reza and Maryam say they love each other and do not want to call it off. Shirin must decide how to frame her advice in today's session and whether to counsel against the marriage.
options: State the risks clearly and recommend against marriage, giving priority to preventing disease in future children.
Describe the risks and options such as prenatal testing and leave the decision to the couple, respecting their autonomy.
Encourage a family meeting where she explains the risks to the elders, trying to bring in the people whose beliefs shape the decision.

title: The Funeral Feast Debt
scenario: After her husband's death in a Bolivian highland village, Basilia Mamani is expected to host a three-day funeral feast with food, drink and music for the whole community. She has no savings and the feast could cost a year's income. Her son Rene, 22, a student in La Paz, urges her to hold a simple service. The village priest and neighbours say a small funeral dishonours the dead. Basilia must announce her plans tomorrow.
options: Hold the full feast on credit, honouring the community norm and her husband's standing even if debt follows.
Hold a simple service as Rene suggests, protecting her finances and risking criticism from neighbours.
Hold a modest feast with contributions from neighbours as is traditional, trusting reciprocity but accepting future obligations.

title: Vows in the Convent Garden
scenario: Sister Agnes Mbeki, novice mistress of a convent in Johannesburg, is approached by Nomsa, 24, a novice who has begun to doubt her calling. Nomsa's family, who have invested heavily in her studies, are proud that she will take final vows next month. Nomsa asks Sister Agnes not to tell her family about her doubts, but the vow ceremony is imminent. Agnes must decide how to counsel Nomsa and whether to delay the ceremony.
options: Advise Nomsa to postpone the vows for discernment, even if it disappoints her family and the community.
Encourage Nomsa to proceed, suggesting that doubts are normal and may pass, respecting her original commitment.
Tell Nomsa the decision must be hers alone and refuse to influence it, while keeping her confidence from the family.

title: The Teacher and the Evolution Chapter
scenario: Hamza Rashid teaches biology at a small Muslim private school in Birmingham. Parent pressure is growing for him to skip the evolution chapter, which will appear on national exams. The headteacher is hesitant to intervene. A bright student, Zainab, 15, privately asks him to teach it fully, saying she wants to be a doctor. Hamza has a few days to decide how to teach the unit.
options: Teach the chapter in full as the exam requires, treating students' educational rights as paramount.
Teach it with explicit framing of how scholars within the faith community engage with the science, trying to bridge both worlds.
Skip detailed teaching and offer optional after-school sessions, reducing conflict but unevenly serving students.

title: Dowry Refused at the Wedding
scenario: Samir Gupta, 30, an accountant in Lucknow, is about to marry Pooja. His parents have quietly asked her family for a significant dowry as part of tradition, though Samir has told them he opposes it. Pooja's father, a modest clerk, has taken a loan to pay. Samir learns of it two days before the wedding. If he refuses the money publicly, his parents will be humiliated; if he stays silent, her family will be indebted. He must decide now.
options: Refuse the dowry in front of the guests, standing on principle and relieving Pooja's family regardless of his parents' shame.
Accept it quietly and return it to Pooja's family afterward, avoiding a scene while correcting the wrong.
Speak privately to his father before the ceremony and insist on returning it, risking a standoff but sparing a public scene.

title: A Haircut for the Mourning Month
scenario: Wanjiru Kamau, a Kenyan accountant in Minneapolis, loses her father back in Nyeri. Family tradition requires that all children return for the burial and for several weeks of mourning. Her employer is in the middle of an audit; she has also just started a new job with no leave. Her brother in Nairobi says she must come or she will be seen as having abandoned the family. Wanjiru has to tell her boss and her family her plan today.
options: Fly home for the full mourning period, honouring the family expectation even at risk to her job.
Attend the burial for a few days and return, balancing family obligation and work security.
Stay in Minneapolis and take part by video, accepting criticism but protecting her livelihood and visa situation.

title: No Photographs, No Phones
scenario: Elder Ruth Zook leads a small Old Order Mennonite community in Pennsylvania. A 17-year-old, Jacob, has secretly used a library computer to study for a high school equivalency, hoping to leave for college. His parents, devout and loving, discover the evidence and ask Ruth to counsel him. The community's rule is that higher schooling leads away from the church. Ruth knows leaving would cause Jacob's family grief. She must decide how to speak with him.
options: Support Jacob's pursuit of education, believing a conscience compelled is no true faith and that he should be free to go.
Urge Jacob to stay in the community, appealing to his faith, family and the life he knows, believing this is what is best for him.
Listen without advising and tell his parents she will not report on his private study, preserving trust and avoiding a forced decision.

title: The Bride Who Wants Both Ceremonies
scenario: Ayesha Siddiqui, 26, a pharmacist in Dubai, wants a civil ceremony for her wedding to Daniel Reyes, a Filipino Catholic, as well as a religious ceremony in her mosque. The imam requires Daniel to convert for the mosque ceremony. Daniel is willing to convert for her but admits it would be a formality. Ayesha's aunt Hafsa, who is close to her, is asked to give her view. Hafsa must decide what to say to Ayesha.
options: Tell Ayesha that a conversion without belief is dishonest and she should choose the civil ceremony alone.
Tell her that many families accept formal conversions as a path to eventual faith and she should take the mosque ceremony.
Tell her she should ask the imam about alternatives, such as a non-convert nikah where permitted, without pushing a view.

title: The Shaman's Invitation
scenario: Seo-yeon Park, 36, a hospital nurse in Busan, finds that her mother has quietly commissioned a gut ritual by a shaman to relieve Seo-yeon's infertility. Seo-yeon is a practising Presbyterian and her pastor warns against such rites. Her mother, aging and anxious, has paid a deposit and is overjoyed at what she calls a gift. Seo-yeon must decide whether to attend the ritual next Saturday.
options: Attend to honour her mother's love, interpreting the rite as cultural and not a betrayal of her faith.
Decline, explaining that it contradicts her convictions, and accept her mother's disappointment and the wasted deposit.
Attend only as an observer, taking no part in the offerings, trying to respect both her mother and her conscience.

title: The Last Rites of a Lapsed Man
scenario: Father Liam Doherty, a hospital chaplain in Cork, is called to a dying 68-year-old man, Tomas, who has long rejected the Church. Tomas's devout sister begs Liam to administer the last rites. Tomas, weak but lucid, tells Liam he wants no priest. The sister says Tomas is not himself. Liam has minutes before Tomas may lose consciousness. He must decide what, if anything, to do.
options: Respect Tomas's refusal and offer only quiet companionship, honouring his stated will.
Administer the rite on the sister's insistence, believing the spiritual stakes outweigh his refusal.
Sit with Tomas and ask whether he would accept a prayer or blessing short of the full sacrament.

title: Burning the Family Photographs
scenario: Sokha Chea, 45, a Cambodian-American in Long Beach, is asked by her devout Buddhist aunt to burn photographs of an ancestor as a merit offering. The photographs, however, are the only images of her grandfather who died under the Khmer Rouge, and her cousin Vireak, a historian, wants to preserve them. The aunt says the ancestor's spirit needs the offering. Sokha, who holds the box, must decide before the memorial next Sunday.
options: Burn them as the aunt asks, putting the spiritual needs of the ancestor ahead of archival value.
Digitise the photographs first, then burn the originals, trying to serve both ritual and memory.
Give them to Vireak for the archive and tell her aunt honestly, accepting the aunt's grief.

title: A Gift of Kidney, A Matter of Caste
scenario: Dr. Rakesh Menon, a transplant coordinator in Thiruvananthapuram, is told by a patient, Gopalan, 55, that his only compatible donor is a distant relative of a lower caste whom Gopalan's family considers impure. Gopalan's wife refuses to allow the donation, while Gopalan, facing death, is willing. The donor, Suresh, has volunteered freely. Dr. Menon must decide whether to proceed when the family is divided.
options: Proceed with the transplant, treating the patient's and donor's consent as sufficient and the wife's objection as non-binding.
Delay until the wife consents, honouring family unity and the risk of postoperative conflict and neglect.
Offer counselling to the whole family before deciding, accepting a delay that may worsen Gopalan's condition.

title: The Altar Boy Strike
scenario: Teodor Ionescu, a Romanian Orthodox priest in a mountain parish, is asked by thirteen-year-old Matei to excuse him from serving at services because he is questioning belief. Matei's father, a church warden, would be embarrassed, and the parish already lacks servers. Matei says he attends only to please his family. Teodor must decide whether to release Matei and what to say to the father.
options: Release Matei from service, treating sincere participation as more important than numbers or appearances.
Ask Matei to continue for a few months while he explores his questions, valuing community belonging as part of the path.
Talk to the father first and propose a conversation among all three, aiming at understanding before any decision.

title: Eating Together at the Wedding
scenario: Lerato Mokoena, a bridesmaid in Gaborone, discovers that the groom's side plans a ritual in which the bride is to kneel and serve the male relatives for several hours as a traditional act of respect. The bride, Tshepiso, a lawyer, finds it demeaning but is afraid to refuse. Lerato, her best friend and master of ceremonies, is asked to run the programme. She must decide whether to omit, modify or run the ritual as planned.
options: Run the ritual as planned, respecting the bride's family and cultural expectations, and letting Tshepiso decide if she objects.
Quietly shorten and soften the ritual, and tell the groom's relatives it is for time reasons, protecting Tshepiso without open conflict.
Urge Tshepiso to talk with her groom to cancel the ritual, offering to back her publicly but leaving the decision to her.
tension: respect for elders vs. friend's autonomy

title: The Vegetarian Grandchild
scenario: Ravindra Kapoor's grandson Arjun, 16, in Leicester, has decided to eat meat after a lifetime of strictly vegetarian upbringing in a Jain family. Arjun's mother is tolerant, but Ravindra, 74, considers the choice a grave sin and has threatened to stop attending family meals. Arjun's friends invite him for a barbecue this weekend. Arjun's uncle Vinod, who speaks to both, must decide what to say to Ravindra.
options: Defend Arjun's right to eat as he chooses, even if Ravindra withdraws from family events.
Ask Arjun to avoid meat in front of Ravindra, respecting the grandfather's beliefs while allowing freedom elsewhere.
Suggest Arjun and Ravindra talk about the reasons behind Arjun's choice, trying to build understanding without forcing an answer.
